mainTopic: How much a worker may eat on the job, and whether the food he eats is his own or a right given by the Torah
overview: The עמוד opens by finishing an earlier point: a worker walking between rows counts as working. It then rereads the משנה so that a donkey may eat from its load until it is unloaded, and shows a ברייתא teaching the same rule. A new משנה says a worker may eat even a דינר's worth of cucumbers or dates. רבי אלעזר חסמא limits him to his wages, while חכמים allow more but warn him not to be greedy. The גמרא gives three ways the תנא קמא and חכמים differ: the advice not to be greedy, רב אסי's rulings about a single cluster, or איסי בן יהודה's view that anyone entering a vineyard may eat, which רב rejects. Next the גמרא asks whether a worker eats from his own or משל שמים, a right the Torah gave him. The practical case is a worker who asks that his share go to his wife and children. Proofs from the משנה and from ברייתות about this case are each pushed off, mostly by explaining them as a נזיר worker who is kept away from vineyards. A new proof from a משנה about a worker preparing figs begins at the end and continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: Walking between rows counts as working
steps.stepSummary: The earlier answer ends: a worker who walks from row to row is treated as someone doing work.
steps.simpleTranslation: And someone walking is considered like someone doing work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the answer it gave just before this. It explains why the worker needed a special enactment to eat while walking between rows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A worker busy with one vine may not eat from a different vine. Walking between rows counts as part of his work, so without the חכמים's enactment he would not be allowed to eat while walking.

keyTerms.meaning: Walking (here, going from row to row)

steps.whatToRemember: Walking between rows counts as work, so eating while walking needed a special enactment of חכמים.

phrases.english: And one who is walking is considered like one doing work.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the answer that started before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Walking between rows has the status of working, so eating then is allowed only because of the enactment.

steps.title: How can a donkey eat while it is being unloaded?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that a donkey may eat 'when it is being unloaded' and asks how that could work.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says a donkey may eat when it is being unloaded. But when it is being unloaded, from where can it eat?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line of the משנה and points out that its wording does not make sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While the load is being taken off the donkey's back, the food is being removed from it. So 'when it is being unloaded' seems to describe a moment when the donkey has nothing left to eat.

keyTerms.meaning: Being unloaded, having its load taken off

phrases.english: The משנה said: And with a donkey, when it is being unloaded.
When it is being unloaded, from where can it eat?!
phrases.notes: The load is the food. Once it is being taken off, the donkey has nothing to eat from.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: At the time of unloading the food is being removed, so the donkey cannot eat from it.

steps.title: Read it as 'until it is unloaded'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the reading: the donkey may eat until the load is taken off.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: until it is unloaded.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading the משנה a little differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה does not mean the moment of unloading. It means the donkey may eat from its load the whole time it carries it, up until the unloading.

phrases.english: Say instead: until it is unloaded.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the wording of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to allow eating only at the moment of unloading, which is impossible.
steps.terutzMaskana: The donkey may eat from its load as long as it carries it, until it is unloaded.

steps.title: Our משנה teaches the same rule as a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the משנה, read this way, matches a ברייתא: a donkey and a camel may eat from their load, but the owner may not hand-feed them.
steps.simpleTranslation: We already learned this in our משנה, as the חכמים taught in a ברייתא: A donkey and a camel may eat from the load on their backs, as long as he does not take food in his hand and feed them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the new reading of the משנה matches a ברייתא that says the same thing openly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא confirms that the animal may eat from its load while carrying it. It adds a limit: the animal may help itself, but the owner may not take the food and feed it by hand.

keyTerms.meaning: We have already learned this (in our משנה)

phrases.english: We have learned in our משנה what the חכמים taught:
A donkey and a camel may eat
from the load that is on their backs,
as long as he does not take it in his hand and feed them.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the animal's owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the new reading with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: Reading the משנה as 'until it is unloaded'
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא: חמור וגמל אוכלים ממשאוי שעל גביהן
steps.whatToRemember: An animal may eat from its load the whole time it carries it, but the owner may not hand-feed it.

steps.title: How much may a worker eat?
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה: a worker may eat cucumbers or dates even worth a דינר. רבי אלעזר חסמא limits him to the value of his wages; חכמים allow more, but we teach him not to be greedy.
steps.simpleTranslation: A worker may eat cucumbers even worth a דינר, and dates even worth a דינר. רבי אלעזר חסמא says: A worker may not eat more than his wages, and the חכמים permit it. But we teach a person not to be a glutton and close the door in his own face.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It sets how much a worker may eat from the crop he works with, and records a dispute about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion allows eating even a lot, worth a whole דינר. רבי אלעזר חסמא caps it at the worker's wages, and חכמים allow it. The closing line gives advice: a greedy worker will find that no one wants to hire him.
steps.confusionAlert: כותבת here means dates (a fruit), not a כתובה. And 'בדינר' means the food is worth a דינר, which is a lot of food.

phrases.english: MISHNA: A worker may eat cucumbers
even worth a דינר,
or dates, even worth a דינר.
רבי אלעזר חסמא says:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יֹאכַל פּוֹעֵל יָתֵר עַל שְׂכָרוֹ,
phrases.english: A worker may not eat more than his wages,
and the חכמים permit it.
But we teach a person
not to be a glutton
and close the door in his own face.
phrases.notes: If he eats greedily, people won't want to hire him again.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ אוֹכֵל פּוֹעֵל קִישּׁוּת אֲפִילּוּ בְּדִינָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new question: the amount a worker may eat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker may eat even a large amount. רבי אלעזר חסמא limits it to his wages, and חכמים permit more, while advising him not to be greedy.

steps.title: Aren't חכמים saying the same as the תנא קמא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה lists חכמים separately when they seem to say exactly what the first opinion said.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים are the same as the תנא קמא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the structure of the משנה: two opinions seem to say the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא allows eating even worth a דינר, without a limit. חכמים 'permit' it too, so the משנה seems to repeat the same opinion for no reason.

keyTerms.meaning: The first opinion in the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: The חכמים are the same as the first opinion?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the משנה just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The opinion of חכמים in the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה would not list the same opinion twice under two names.

steps.title: The difference is 'we teach a person'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two opinions differ over the advice not to be greedy: the תנא קמא does not hold of it, and חכמים do.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is 'but we teach'. The תנא קמא does not hold of 'we teach'. The חכמים do hold of 'we teach'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by showing a real difference between the two opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions allow the worker to eat a lot. Only חכמים add that we warn him not to be greedy; the תנא קמא gives no such warning. So the closing line of the משנה belongs to חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them
He does not hold of it

steps.whatToRemember: The תנא קמא and חכמים both allow a worker to eat a lot. Only חכמים add the advice not to be greedy.

phrases.english: The difference between them is 'but we teach':
The first opinion does not hold of 'we teach'.
The חכמים do hold of 'we teach'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finding a practical difference between the two opinions
steps.terutzHavaAmina: חכמים seemed to say exactly what the תנא קמא said.
steps.terutzMaskana: They differ only over the advice 'מלמדין': חכמים hold of it, and the תנא קמא does not.

steps.title: Another answer: they differ over רב אסי's rulings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a second answer: the תנא קמא and חכמים differ over two rulings of רב אסי. A worker may eat even if he was hired to harvest only one cluster, and he may eat even if he harvested only one cluster so far.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say the difference between them is about רב אסי's rule. רב אסי said: even if he hired him to harvest only one cluster, the worker may eat it. And רב אסי also said: even if he harvested only one cluster, he may eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer to the question of step 6. The two opinions in the משנה argue about רב אסי's rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 7 the difference was the advice not to be greedy. Here the גמרא offers another option: one of the two opinions holds like רב אסי, and the other does not. רב אסי says a worker may eat even when the whole job, or the work done so far, is only one cluster.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say: the opening of another possible answer

steps.confusionAlert: רב אסי gave two rulings that sound alike. The first is about being HIRED for only one cluster. The second is about having HARVESTED only one cluster so far.

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
The difference between them is the ruling of Rav Asi.
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the תנא קמא and חכמים in the משנה.

phrases.english: As Rav Asi said:
Even if he hired him only
to harvest one cluster, he may eat it.
And Rav Asi also said:
Even if he harvested only
one cluster, he may eat it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ דְּרַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the קשיא of step 6, in place of step 7's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: Why does the משנה list חכמים separately if they say the same as the תנא קמא?
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying a practical difference between the opinions
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תנא קמא and חכמים seem to say exactly the same thing.
steps.terutzMaskana: They differ over whether a worker may eat when only one cluster is involved, following רב אסי.

steps.title: Why רב אסי needed to say both rulings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that both of רב אסי's rulings are needed. Each case has a reason you might allow eating that does not apply to the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both rulings are needed. If he had taught only the first one, I would say the worker may eat because there is nothing else to put into the owner's baskets. But where there is still more to put in, I would say he should first put some in and only then eat. And if he had taught only the second one, I would say he may eat because he can still finish the job at the end. But where he can't finish the job at the end, I would say no. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks itself why רב אסי said two rulings that look so similar. It answers that you could not learn one from the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Case 1, hired for one cluster: eating seems allowed only because nothing else is left to do. So you might think that when there is still work, he must put some in the owner's baskets first. Case 2, harvested one so far: eating seems allowed because he can still do his job afterward. So you might think that when eating the one cluster ends the whole job, it is forbidden. Each ruling closes a different gap.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was necessary: both statements are needed
The owner's vessels or baskets, where the harvested fruit goes
To fulfill, to carry out his job

steps.confusionAlert: Each 'I would say' is a mistaken thought the גמרא rejects. The actual law follows both rulings: the worker may eat in both cases.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic צריכותא: the גמרא shows that two rulings that seem alike each teach something new.

phrases.english: And both were necessary,
for if he had taught us only that first one,
phrases.notes: The first one is the worker who was hired to harvest just one cluster.

phrases.english: I would say he may eat because there is nothing
to put into the owner's vessels.
But where there is something
to put into the owner's vessels,
I would say he should first put some in, and then eat.
And if he had taught us only this one,
I would say he may eat because he can still do the job at the end,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא דְּלָא אֶפְשָׁר לְקַיּוֹמֵי לְבַסּוֹף –
phrases.english: but here, where he cannot do the job at the end,
phrases.notes: If his whole job is one cluster and he eats it, nothing is left to put in the baskets.

phrases.english: I would say no. So both are necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why רב אסי's two rulings, quoted in step 8, are not repeating each other.
steps.kashyaTarget: An unspoken question: why did רב אסי need two such similar rulings?
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing each statement is necessary
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One ruling could be learned from the other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each case has its own reason for allowing eating, so neither can be learned from the other.

steps.title: A third answer: they differ over איסי בן יהודה's teaching
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a third answer: the difference between the opinions is a teaching of רב. In a hidden scroll in רבי חייא's house, רב found that איסי בן יהודה says the פסוק 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard' speaks of any person who enters.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say the difference between them is about רב's teaching. רב said: I found a hidden scroll in רבי חייא's house, and in it was written: איסי בן יהודה says, 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard': the פסוק is speaking about anyone who comes in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more possible answer to step 6's question. It brings a teaching רב found written in a hidden scroll.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the פסוק about eating in a vineyard is read as speaking about a worker. איסי בן יהודה reads it as speaking about any person who enters. The גמרא suggests that one opinion in the משנה holds this way and the other does not.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא whose teaching was written in the scroll
When you come into your neighbor's vineyard (דברים 23:25)
About the entry of any person

steps.whyThisMatters: איסי בן יהודה's reading is a big change: the right to eat would not belong only to a worker. The next step brings רב's reaction, which shows how the two opinions in the משנה line up.

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
The difference between them is the teaching of Rav.
As Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: מָצָאתִי מְגִילַּת סְתָרִים בֵּי רַבִּי חִיָּיא,
phrases.english: I found a hidden scroll in Rabbi Chiya's house,
and written in it was:
Isi ben Yehuda says:
'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard':
phrases.notes: דברים 23:25

phrases.english: the verse is speaking about any person who comes in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a third possible answer to step 6's קשיא, in place of the answers about greed and רב אסי.
steps.kashyaTarget: Why does the משנה list חכמים separately if they say the same as the תנא קמא?
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying a practical difference between the opinions
steps.terutzMaskana: They may differ over איסי בן יהודה's reading that the פסוק speaks of any person entering a vineyard.

steps.title: רב's reaction: איסי leaves owners with nothing
steps.stepSummary: רב reacts to איסי בן יהודה's teaching by saying it would leave no one able to make a living. This completes the third answer: the תנא קמא agrees with רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב said: איסי has not left a livelihood for any creature.
steps.whatsHappening: רב reacts to the teaching he found from איסי בן יהודה and says that if anyone can eat, owners would be ruined. This finishes the third answer from step 10.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 10, רב quoted איסי בן יהודה: the פסוק about entering a vineyard covers any person. Here רב says this cannot be practical, since passersby would eat everything. So the תנא קמא follows רב (only workers may eat), and חכמים follow איסי.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the third answer works. The two opinions in the משנה follow two sides: רב's view and איסי's view.

phrases.english: And Rav said:
Isi has not left a livelihood
phrases.notes: This is איסי בן יהודה from the hidden scroll in step 10.

phrases.english: for any creature.
phrases.notes: He means if every passerby may eat, the owner's whole crop would be eaten up.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב: לָא שְׁבַק אִיסִי חַיֵּי לְכׇל בְּרִיָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the third answer begun in step 10 by giving רב's reaction, which matches the תנא קמא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies the dispute between the תנא קמא and חכמים as the dispute between רב and איסי בן יהודה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תנא קמא and חכמים seem to say the same thing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תנא קמא follows רב (only hired workers eat). חכמים follow איסי (anyone entering may eat).

steps.title: רב אשי suggests איסי meant only volunteers who work
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי tells over that he suggested to רב כהנא a softer reading of איסי: maybe he meant only people who come in, work, and eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: I said this teaching before רב כהנא and asked: perhaps איסי means those who work for their meal, who work and eat?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי pushes back on רב's complaint by suggesting איסי was not talking about everyone, only people who come in on their own to work. This sets up רב כהנא's reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If איסי meant only volunteers who actually do the work, then רב's worry that owners will be ruined seems weaker. The owner is getting work done in exchange for the fruit eaten.

keyTerms.meaning: before him, in front of him
working for their meal (working only in exchange for eating)

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
I said this teaching
before Rav Kahana:
perhaps it is about those who work for their meal,
who work and eat?
phrases.notes: These people walk in on their own, nobody hired them, and they pick in exchange for eating.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי, אַמְרִיתַהּ לִשְׁמַעְתָּא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא: דִּלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's complaint in step 11 by reading איסי more narrowly.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that איסי's view leaves owners with nothing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If איסי only allows people who actually work to eat, the owner gets labor in return, so he is not being ruined.

steps.title: רב כהנא: an owner prefers to pick his own workers
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא answers that even so, an owner wants to hire his own workers for his orchard, not have everyone come in.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to me: Even so, a person prefers to hire workers to pick his orchard, rather than have everyone come in and eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא defends רב's complaint: even volunteer workers are a problem for the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner wants control over who works his field. Strangers walking in to work and eat take that control away. So רב's complaint about איסי still stands even with רב אשי's narrower reading.

keyTerms.meaning: he prefers, it is pleasing to him

steps.whatToRemember: The third answer stands. רב (and the תנא קמא) hold that only hired workers may eat, because an owner does not want just anyone, even a worker, coming in on his own.

phrases.english: He said to me:
phrases.notes: "He" is רב כהנא answering רב אשי.

phrases.english: Even so,
a person prefers
to hire workers
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets; the words in square brackets are the corrected wording. Both mean the same thing.

phrases.english: and have them pick his orchard,
and not have everyone come (and eat it).
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the words in round brackets.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לִי: אֲפִילּוּ הָכִי, נִיחָא לֵיהּ לְאִינִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's suggestion in step 12 and upholds רב's complaint.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reasoning about what an owner wants.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If איסי only meant volunteers who work, the owner loses nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: An owner still wants to choose his own workers, so איסי's view still hurts him.

steps.title: Does a worker eat from his own or from Heaven's?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: when a worker eats on the job, is that food his own, or is it a special right the Torah gave him?
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked among them: Does a worker eat from his own, or does he eat from what belongs to Heaven?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a brand new question about the nature of the worker's right to eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two ways to see it: (1) the food is like part of his pay, so it really belongs to him; or (2) the Torah gave him a personal permission to eat, but the food is not truly his.

keyTerms.meaning: a question was asked among them (an open question)
from Heaven's (a gift from the Torah)

phrases.english: A question was asked among them:
Does a worker eat from his own,
phrases.notes: He means the food is truly his, like part of his pay.

phrases.english: or does he eat from what belongs to Heaven?
phrases.notes: He means the Torah gave him a personal right to eat, but the food isn't really his.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: פּוֹעֵל מִשֶּׁלּוֹ הוּא אוֹכֵל, אוֹ מִשֶּׁל שָׁמַיִם הוּא אוֹכֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of the תנא קמא and חכמים ends.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the food a worker eats on the job belongs to him or is a personal right granted by the Torah.

steps.title: What is the practical difference?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference this question makes.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference does it make?
steps.whatsHappening: Before trying to answer, the גמרא asks where this question would actually matter. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants a real case where the two views lead to different results. Only then is the question worth working on.

keyTerms.meaning: what practical difference comes out of it?

phrases.english: What difference does it make?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical result of the question in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where it matters whether the worker eats from his own or from Heaven's.

steps.title: The case: a worker asks to give his share to his family
steps.stepSummary: The difference is when the worker says, 'Give my share to my wife and children.' If the food is his, they get it. If it is a personal right from the Torah, they do not. The question stays open.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he says: Give to my wife and children. If you say he eats from his own, we give to them. But if you say he eats from Heaven's, the Torah gave the right only to him, not to his wife and children. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the practical case: a worker who wants his family to eat in his place. Then it asks again what the law is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the food is truly the worker's, he can pass it to anyone, including his family. If it is only a personal permission from the Torah, it cannot be handed to others. The step ends with מאי, meaning the question is still not answered.

keyTerms.meaning: the Torah gave him the right

steps.confusionAlert: The step ends with מאי, so nothing has been decided yet. The גמרא has only explained why the question matters.

phrases.english: When he says: Give to my wife and children.
If you say he eats from his own,
we give to them.
But if you say
he eats from Heaven's,
the Torah gave the right to him,

phrases.aramaic: לְאִשְׁתּוֹ וּבָנָיו – לָא זַכִּי לְהוּ רַחֲמָנָא,
phrases.english: to his wife and children the Torah did not give the right.
What is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15 by giving the practical case, then repeats the open question from step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The difference is whether a worker may have his wife and children eat his share in his place.

steps.title: A worker may eat even more than his wage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to prove from the משנה that the food is not his own, since a worker may eat far more than he is paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a worker may eat cucumbers, or dates, even if they are worth a whole דינר. If the food were truly his own, how could someone hired for a sixth of a דינר get to eat a whole דינר's worth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a rule from the משנה to try to answer the question: the worker may eat more than his whole wage. That seems to show the food is not 'his own.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that if the food were the worker's own property, like part of his pay, it should not be worth more than his pay. Since he may eat much more than he earns, the proof says it must be a special right from Heaven instead.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source as proof
One-sixth of a דינר, a small coin
A זוז, the same as a דינר

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A worker may eat cucumbers
even if they are worth a dinar,
or dates, even if they are worth a dinar.
If you say he is eating from his own,
he was hired for a sixth of a dinar, and he eats a whole zuz's worth?!
phrases.notes: A זוז and a דינר are the same coin, so he would be eating six times his pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to settle the open question from steps 14-16.
steps.raayaObject: That the worker eats משל שמים (by a Torah right), not from his own.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's rule that a worker may eat even a dinar's worth of cucumbers or dates.

steps.title: The same problem exists either way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off the proof: even if the food is from Heaven, he still eats more than his wage, so the Torah simply gave him that right.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what would you say instead, that he eats from Heaven's property? Either way, a man hired for a sixth of a דינר is eating a whole דינר! You have to say the Torah gave him that right. So here too, the Torah gave him the right to own that much.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 17. It shows that the 'eats more than his wage' problem fits both sides equally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under either view he eats more than his pay, so that fact cannot decide between them. The answer is the same for both: רחמנא gave it to him. If the Torah can give him a right worth more than his wage, it can also give him ownership worth more than his wage.

keyTerms.meaning: From Heaven's property: a special right the Torah gave, not his own
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: But rather, what would you say?
That he eats from Heaven's property?

phrases.aramaic: סוֹף סוֹף אֲגִיר בְּדַנְקָא אָכֵיל בְּזוּזָא!
phrases.english: In the end, he is still hired for a sixth of a dinar and eats a whole zuz's worth!
So what do you have to say?
That the Merciful One gave him the right.
Here too, the Merciful One gave him the right.
phrases.notes: He means that even if the food counts as his own, the Torah can give him ownership of more than his wage.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא מַאי – מִשֶּׁל שָׁמַיִם הוּא אוֹכֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 17.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from 'eating more than his wage.'
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The problem fits both sides equally, and the same answer (the Torah gave it to him) works for both.

steps.title: Maybe רבי אלעזר חסמא and the חכמים argue about this exact question
steps.stepSummary: A second proof: רבי אלעזר חסמא limits the worker to his wage and the חכמים do not. Maybe that is the same as our question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי אלעזר חסמא says a worker may not eat more than his wage, and the חכמים allow it. Isn't this what they argue about? One holds he eats from his own, and the other holds he eats from Heaven's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new proof. It suggests that our question is really the argument in the משנה between רבי אלעזר חסמא and the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the food is his own, like part of his pay, it makes sense to cap it at his wage, which is רבי אלעזר חסמא's view. If it is a gift from Heaven, there is no reason to tie it to his wage, which is the חכמים' view. That would show the question is a real argument between תנאים.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא in the משנה who limits how much the worker may eat
Isn't this what they argue about?

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע, רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר חַסָּמָא אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: Come and hear: רבי אלעזר חסמא says:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יֹאכַל פּוֹעֵל יוֹתֵר עַל שְׂכָרוֹ,
phrases.english: A worker may not eat more than his wage,
and the חכמים permit it.
Isn't this what they argue about?
One master holds he eats from his own,
phrases.notes: This one is רבי אלעזר חסמא.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר מִשֶּׁל שָׁמַיִם הוּא אוֹכֵל.
phrases.english: and the other master holds he eats from Heaven's property.
phrases.notes: This one is the חכמים.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר חַסָּמָא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof fails, a second proof is offered.
steps.raayaObject: That the question 'his own or Heaven's' is the subject of a תנאים argument.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's argument between רבי אלעזר חסמא and the חכמים.

steps.title: No, they argue about the word כנפשך
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: everyone may agree he eats from his own, and the argument is about how to read כנפשך. רבי אלעזר reads it as 'what he risks his life for.'
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees he eats from his own, and here they argue about the word 'כנפשך.' One master holds that כנפשך means: for the thing he risks his life over.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the second proof. It gives a different reason for the argument, starting with רבי אלעזר חסמא's reading of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now both sides hold the food is his own, so their argument tells us nothing about our question. רבי אלעזר reads כנפשך as 'what he puts his life on the line for,' meaning his wage. So his eating is tied to his wage and cannot go above it.

keyTerms.meaning: A word in the פסוק about the worker eating; literally 'like your soul'
Risks his life, puts himself on the line

steps.confusionAlert: This does not answer our question either way. It only shows that this argument may not be about it.

phrases.aramaic: לָא דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מִשֶּׁלּוֹ הוּא אוֹכֵל,
phrases.english: No. Everyone agrees he eats from his own,
and here they argue about the word 'כנפשך.'
phrases.notes: דברים 23:25

phrases.english: One master holds: כנפשך means
the thing he risks his life for,
phrases.notes: That is his wage. So he may eat only up to what he is paid.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מִשֶּׁלּוֹ הוּא אוֹכֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 19 by giving another reason for the argument.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that רבי אלעזר חסמא and the חכמים argue about 'his own or Heaven's.'
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Their argument can be explained as a difference in reading the word כנפשך.

steps.title: The חכמים read כנפשך as 'like yourself'
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים read כנפשך as comparing the worker to the owner himself: if you muzzle yourself you are exempt, and the same goes for a worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other master holds כנפשך means 'like yourself': just as with yourself, if you muzzle yourself you are exempt, so too with a worker, if you muzzle him you are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes pushing off the proof by giving the חכמים' reading of the same word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים do not read כנפשך as 'what he risks his life for.' To them it compares the worker to the owner, and from this they learn that there are cases where you may stop a worker from eating. Since they do not get רבי אלעזר's limit from the word, they have no wage cap, and the open question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: You muzzled, you held back from eating

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs were pushed off. We still do not know if the worker eats from his own or by a right from Heaven.

phrases.english: And the other master holds כנפשך means:
just as with yourself, if you muzzled yourself, you are exempt,
phrases.notes: The owner does not have to eat his own fruit, so holding himself back is no sin.

phrases.english: so too a worker, if you muzzled him, you are exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the rejection of step 20 by giving the חכמים' reading.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Completes the rejection of the proof from step 19.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The חכמים read כנפשך differently, so the argument depends on the פסוק and not on 'his own or Heaven's.'

steps.title: Proof from a נזיר who asks to give his share to his family
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says a נזיר who asks that his portion go to his wife and children is not listened to. If a worker eats from his own, why not?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a נזיר who said 'Give to my wife and my children,' they do not listen to him. If you say the worker eats from his own, why don't they listen to him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new proof that the worker's food is not his own. A נזיר worker may not give his share to his family.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נזיר working in a vineyard cannot eat the grapes himself, so he asks that they go to his family instead. If the food really belonged to him, he could hand it to anyone. Since he cannot, it seems the food is only a right to eat, not something he owns.

keyTerms.meaning: A nazirite, forbidden to eat grapes and anything from the vine
Give it to my wife and my children
We do not listen to him

phrases.english: Come and hear: a nazirite who said
phrases.notes: He is working in a vineyard. He can't eat the grapes himself, so he asks that they go to his family.

phrases.english: "Give to my wife and my children"
they do not listen to him.
And if you say he eats from his own,
why do they not listen to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proofs in steps 17-21 were rejected, a new proof is brought, this time using the very case from step 16: asking that the share go to his wife and children.
steps.raayaObject: That the worker eats from Heaven's gift (משל שמים), not from his own
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a נזיר who may not give his share to his family

steps.title: The נזיר is kept away from the vineyard
steps.stepSummary: The rule for the נזיר has a special reason: we push a נזיר away from vineyards. It has nothing to do with who owns the food.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it is because of 'Go, go, we say to a נזיר: go around, go around, do not come near the vineyard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof. The נזיר case has its own reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We don't want a נזיר taking a job in a vineyard, where he might be tempted to eat grapes. So חכמים take away any benefit: his family may not get his share. This tells us nothing about ordinary workers.

phrases.english: There, it is because of "Go, go,"
we say to a nazirite:
"Go around, go around; do not come near the vineyard."

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, מִשּׁוּם לָךְ לָךְ אָמְרִין נְזִירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 22
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Full rejection of the נזיר proof
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The rule comes from a special concern to keep a נזיר away from vineyards, not from the rights of a worker

steps.title: Proof from an ordinary worker who asks to give to his family
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא says the same rule about a plain פועל, with no mention of a נזיר. That seems to prove he does not eat from his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a worker who said 'Give to my wife and my children,' they do not listen to him. If he eats from his own, why don't they listen to him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a stronger proof. This ברייתא says 'worker,' not 'nazirite.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer about the נזיר seems not to work here, because the ברייתא speaks of any worker. If even a regular worker cannot give his share away, the food must not be his.

phrases.english: Come and hear: a worker who said
"Give to my wife and my children"
they do not listen to him.
And if you say he eats from his own,
why do they not listen to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new proof that avoids the נזיר answer of step 23
steps.raayaObject: That the worker does not eat from his own
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a plain worker

steps.title: The 'worker' here is a נזיר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the 'worker' in this ברייתא is really a נזיר worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'worker'? A נזיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof by reading 'worker' as a worker who is a נזיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the worker is a נזיר, the reason from step 23 applies again: we keep him away from the vineyard. Then the ברייתא proves nothing about ordinary workers.

keyTerms.meaning: What kind of worker is meant here?

phrases.english: What is meant by "worker"? A nazirite.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 24
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Full rejection by redefining the case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא's 'worker' can be read as a נזיר worker

steps.title: But one teaching says נזיר and another says worker
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: one ברייתא says 'נזיר' and another says 'worker,' so they must be different cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: But one teaching says 'נזיר' and another teaching says 'worker'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer. Different words suggest different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both ברייתות were about a נזיר, why would one say 'worker'? The change in wording seems to show the second one is about any worker.

keyTerms.meaning: But it was taught (in a ברייתא)!
It was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: But it was taught "nazirite,"
and it was taught "worker"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 25
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two different words in two ברייתות suggest two different cases

steps.title: The two teachings were not taught side by side
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two ברייתות were not taught next to each other, so the change in wording proves nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Were they taught next to each other?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Separate teachings can use different words for the same case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A difference in wording only means something when the two lines appear side by side in one teaching. These were two separate ברייתות, so one said 'nazirite' and the other said 'worker,' and both can mean a נזיר worker.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it so that...? (a question expecting 'no')

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא admits these are different cases. It only says the different wording is not a reason to think so.

phrases.english: Were they taught next to each other?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 26
steps.terutzResolutionType: Wording from separate sources is not compared
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The different words mean the cases are different
steps.terutzMaskana: Separate ברייתות may use different words for the same case, a נזיר worker

steps.title: Proof from a verse about workers
steps.stepSummary: A third ברייתא finds the source for the rule in the verse 'into your vessel you shall not put,' which is about workers in general.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: From where do we know that a worker who said 'Give to my wife and my children' is not listened to? As it says: 'But into your vessel you shall not put.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third proof. This ברייתא gives a verse about workers as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the source is a פסוק about any worker, not a rule about a נזיר. That makes it seem like the rule applies to all workers. So the food would not be his own.

phrases.english: Come and hear: From where do we know, regarding a worker
who said "Give to my wife and my children,"
that they do not listen to him?
As it says: "But into your vessel you shall not put."
phrases.notes: דברים 23:25

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new proof whose source is a verse about workers
steps.raayaObject: That the worker does not eat from his own
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that learns the rule from the פסוק about a worker's vessel

steps.title: Blocking the nazirite answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks the answer that this is a נזיר. For a נזיר the reason would be 'go, go,' not this verse.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say this too is a נזיר: if so, is the reason 'into your vessel you shall not put'? The reason would be 'go, go, we say to a נזיר'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers ahead of time the expected push-off. The verse does not fit a נזיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the case were a נזיר, the ברייתא would give the 'keep away from the vineyard' reason. Since it quotes a פסוק about workers, it seems to mean all workers. This makes the proof of step 28 stronger.

phrases.english: And if you would say: here too it means a nazirite,

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי מִשּׁוּם ״אֶל כֶּלְיְךָ לֹא תִּתֵּן״,
phrases.english: if so, is it because of "into your vessel you shall not put"?
It is because of "Go, go, we say to a nazirite"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the proof of step 28 by blocking the answer used in step 25
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible answer that this ברייתא also means a נזיר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A נזיר rule would be based on 'go, go,' not on the פסוק about a worker's vessel

steps.title: It is a נזיר, but the verse matches the wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says yes, it really is a נזיר. Since the ברייתא used the word 'worker,' it quoted the verse about workers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, that is indeed so. Since it teaches it using the word 'worker,' it brings the verse about a worker.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the last proof. The case is a נזיר, and the verse is quoted only because the ברייתא said 'worker.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The real reason is still to keep a נזיר away from vineyards. The ברייתא happened to call him a 'worker,' so it quoted the worker's פסוק to match. None of the three ברייתות proves that an ordinary worker eats food that is not his own.
steps.whatToRemember: All three ברייתות saying 'we do not listen to him' are explained as being about a נזיר worker, whom we keep away from vineyards. So the question of whether a worker eats from his own or משל שמים is still not proven.

phrases.english: Yes, that is indeed so,
and since it teaches it in the language of a worker,
it brings the verse about a worker.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין הָכִי נָמֵי, וְאַיְּידֵי דְּקָתָנֵי לַהּ בִּלְשׁוֹן פּוֹעֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of steps 28-29
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Full rejection of the verse-based proof
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The verse is quoted only to match the word 'worker'; the real reason is the rule for a נזיר

steps.title: A new proof begins: the case of hiring a worker to prepare figs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new proof from a משנה, starting with the case of someone who hires a worker to prepare figs for drying.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear a proof: someone who hires a worker to prepare figs for drying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a new proof by quoting the first words of a משנה about a worker hired to prepare figs for drying. This line only sets up the case. The actual details and the proof come in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier proof from the נזיר ברייתא ended without settling the question. Now the גמרא tries a different source, a משנה from מסכת מעשרות. So far we have only the setting: an employer and a worker who handles figs that are being prepared for drying.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear. The usual way the גמרא brings a new proof.
To cut or prepare (figs) for drying

phrases.english: Come and hear:
one who hires a worker
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in מעשרות ב:ז.

phrases.english: to prepare figs for drying

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הַשּׂוֹכֵר אֶת הַפּוֹעֵל לְקַצּוֹת בִּתְאֵנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The proof from the ברייתא about a נזיר who is a worker was turned aside in step 30, so the גמרא now tries a fresh proof from a משנה.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a worker eats from his own (the food is truly his) or משל שמים (a personal right the Torah gave him)
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in מעשרות ב:ז about hiring a worker to prepare figs for drying. Only the opening setup is quoted so far.
